title: More blessed to give (Acts 20:17–38)
hookLine: Paul's farewell at Miletus; they weep and kneel on the shore

lines: YOU WILL NOT SEE MY FACE AGAIN.
cards: A beach at Miletus, on the coast of Asia. Paul is in a hurry to reach Jerusalem, so he doesn't go up to Ephesus, where he spent about three years.

Instead he sends for the elders of the Ephesian church, and they make the journey down to the shore. He tells them plainly: I don't know what will happen to me in Jerusalem, except that prison and hardship are waiting.
And you will not see my face again.

teach.b: Paul's farewell sounds like a man setting his affairs in order. He reminds them how he lived among them: serving the Lord with humility and tears, holding nothing back, teaching in public and from house to house.
He tells them to keep watch over the flock, like shepherds. Then he holds up his hands. I've coveted no one's silver or gold or clothing.

teach.h: THESE HANDS WORKED FOR MY NEEDS.
teach.b: These hands, he says, worked for my own needs and for those who were with me.

teach.h: A SAYING FOUND IN NO GOSPEL.
teach.b: Then he gives them a saying of Jesus, in the Douay-Rheims: "remember the word of the Lord Jesus, how he said: It is a more blessed thing to give, rather than to receive."
Here's the surprise: those words of Jesus aren't in any of the four Gospels. Matthew, Mark, Luke and John never record them.
It's a saying of Jesus preserved only here, in Paul's mouth, passed along by Luke, kept by people who remembered it. And Paul isn't asking the elders for money.
He's showing them his own work-worn hands and saying: this is how to lead. Give. Then the ending.
Paul kneels down on the shore and prays with them all.

teach.h: MORE BLESSED TO GIVE, RATHER THAN TO RECEIVE.
teach.b: They weep, embrace him, and kiss him, grieving most of all, the text says, because he told them they would not see his face again. And they walk him to the ship.

how: Catholics practice almsgiving, one of the three traditional disciplines of Lent alongside prayer and fasting, and give to the poor through parish collections and works of mercy throughout the year.

o: how Jesus calls giving, in a saying kept only in Acts
what Paul called his years of work with his hands in Ephesus
the word Paul used for the elders of the church at Ephesus

games.q: on the shore at Miletus — tap the pairs.
p: a saying of Jesus in no Gospel
where Paul knelt and prayed with them

s: it is more blessed to give than to receive is in one of the Gospels
it isn't in any of the four Gospels. Paul quotes it as Jesus' words in Acts.
Paul asked the elders for money in his farewell
he showed his own hands and said they had worked for his needs.
the elders wept because they would not see him again
that grieved them most of all, the text says.

games.q: you're Paul, saying goodbye forever to people you've taught for three years. what do you leave them?
o: a list of rules to follow.
your example, and a saying of Jesus about giving.
games.why: he points to how he lived, holds up his working hands, and quotes Jesus: it is a more blessed thing to give, rather than to receive.

practice: Look at your hands, the way Paul held up his, and ask what they've given lately.

Think of one thing you could give freely, without being asked, not necessarily money: time, a meal, a compliment you meant to say, help with a task, something you own that someone else needs more, and picture handing it over without waiting for thanks.
If you pray, offer your hands for whatever giving the day brings.

wordCard.voice: Blessed. The word Jesus used in a saying kept only by Paul, on a beach at Miletus: it is more blessed to give than to receive. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek: blessed, the same word family as the Beatitudes. more blessed is it to give.

carryVoice: Your line: coveted no one's silver. Tomorrow, Jerusalem, and the steps of a barracks. Day five hundred fifty-four.

sources.q: remember the word of the Lord Jesus, how he said: It is a more blessed thing to give, rather than to receive.
